s6.quote: Thrice blest are they who never tasted pain!
s6.note: The sisters have just been led indoors under sentence, and Creon probably stays on stage through the song. The Greek is quieter than Storr: εὐδαίμονες (_eudaimones_, 'fortunate, with a good daimon') are those whose life is κακῶν ἄγευστος (_kakon ageustos_, 'without a taste of evils', l. 583). 'Thrice' is Storr's. The ode on man in [[s4]] sang of what man can do; this one, its dark twin, sings of what is done to him.

s6.quote: If once the curse of Heaven attaint a race,
s6.note: Storr's legal 'attaint' hides an earthquake. The Greek says 'those whose house is shaken from the gods', σεισθῇ θεόθεν δόμος (l. 584), and the thing that then never fails them is ἄτας (_atas_, from _ate_: ruin, and the delusion that brings it). That word comes four times in this ode (ll. 584, 614, 623, 625) and is the song's real subject. Note that it is a house, _domos_, that is shaken: the unit of suffering here is the family, never the individual.

s6.quote: The infection lingers on and speeds apace,
s6.note: The Greek has no infection; _ate_ is ἕρπον (_herpon_, 'creeping', l. 585) over the whole length of the family. The verb comes back twice (ll. 613, 617), so that ruin, the law of Zeus and the unwary man's foot all move at the same crawl. It is the idea Antigone opened the play with, the evils that come from Oedipus, but from her it was a grievance and from the elders it is an excuse: if the house is cursed, nobody in the room has to be blamed.

s6.quote: Sweep o’er the blackening main and whirl to land
s6.note: The simile is a Thracian north wind driving a swell across ἔρεβος ὕφαλον (_erebos hyphalon_, 'the darkness under the sea', l. 587). Set it beside the ode on man in [[s4]], where man crosses the grey sea in a winter gale and comes through. Here the same sea is seen from the shore, and nobody is steering anything. I take the pairing as deliberate: Sophocles lets the Chorus unsay its own optimism.

s6.quote: From Ocean’s cavernous depths his ooze and sand,
s6.note: The storm rolls up κελαινὰν θῖνα (_kelainan thina_, 'black sand') from the bottom, βυσσόθεν (_byssothen_, 'from the depths', l. 590). That is the point of the comparison, and Storr keeps it well. What a family curse does is bring up old sediment: things done generations ago, long settled, are churned to the surface and thrown on the present.

s6.quote: Billow on billow thunders on the shore.
s6.note: Storr's 'billow on billow' anticipates the 'woe upon woe' of the next stanza and is not in the Greek. What the Greek has is sound: the headlands, beaten head-on, στόνῳ βρέμουσι (_stonoi bremousi_, 'roar with a groan', l. 591). _Stonos_ is a human noise, the groan of mourning, so the landscape is already lamenting before the Chorus names the family.

s6.quote: On the Labdacidae I see descending
s6.note: Labdacus was the grandfather of Oedipus. The troubles are ἀρχαῖα (_archaia_, 'ancient', l. 593), and they fall 'on the troubles of the dead', πήματα φθιτῶν ἐπὶ πήμασι (l. 595). The elders say 'I see', and what they see is a pattern. Ask what the pattern leaves out: Creon's edict, issued this morning, appears nowhere in their account of why this girl is to die.

s6.quote: Laid on the race a malison, and his rod
s6.note: 'Malison' is the opposite of benison: a curse. The Greek is vaguer and bleaker. 'Generation does not release generation, but some one of the gods strikes them down', θεῶν τις (_theon tis_, l. 597), 'and there is no deliverance', οὐδʼ ἔχει λύσιν. No god is named and no offence is given. The vagueness is the point; a curse with no author needs no remedy and permits no protest.

s6.quote: The light that dawned upon its last born son
s6.note: A mistranslation that matters. The Greek speaks of a light spread over 'the last root' in the house of Oedipus, ἐσχάτας and ῥίζας (ll. 597 and 600), and the last root is Antigone, with Ismene; there is no son. The elders are saying that the family's one remaining hope of continuing was this girl and her marriage. Storr's 'son' sends the reader looking for Polynices or Eteocles and loses the fact that the ode is about the person who has just left the stage.

s6.quote: Is vanished, and the bloody axe of Fate
s6.note: A famous crux. The manuscripts, and the Greek text shown here, read κόνις (_konis_, 'dust', l. 602): 'the bloody dust of the gods below mows it down'. Many editors, Jebb among them, print the conjecture _kopis_, 'chopper', and Storr's 'axe' follows them, since dust is an odd thing to reap with. I would keep the dust. It is the handful Antigone scattered on her brother in [[s3]], the thinnest substance in the play, and the elders are saying that it has cut down a royal house.

s6.quote: Has felled the goodly tree that blossomed late.
s6.note: The tree is half Storr's; the Greek has only the root and the verb ἀμᾷ (_amai_, 'mows, reaps', l. 602). But the instinct is good, because vegetable images are about to matter. In [[s7]] Haemon will show his father trees on a riverbank that survive by bending and others that go under 'root and branch'. The house of Oedipus is already cut to the root; Creon's is still standing and can still choose.

s6.quote: O Oedipus, by reckless pride undone!
s6.note: There is no address to Oedipus in the Greek. The line names the two things that, with the dust, cut the root down: λόγου τʼ ἄνοια (_logou anoia_, 'folly of speech') and φρενῶν ἐρινύς (_phrenon erinys_, 'a Fury of the mind', l. 602). This is the elders' judgment on Antigone: her defiant speech to Creon in [[s5]] was mindlessness, and the avenging spirit of the family now lives inside her head. It is the first of this stretch's many verdicts on who has _phrenes_, good sense, and who has lost them.

s6.quote: Thy might, O Zeus, what mortal power can quell?
s6.note: Storr's 'mortal power' translates ὑπερβασία (_hyperbasia_, 'overstepping, transgression', l. 605): what human trespass could hold down the power of Zeus? The word is loaded. Creon asked Antigone in [[s5]] whether she had dared to overstep his laws, and in [[s7]] he will damn anyone who 'oversteps' and forces the law (l. 663). The Chorus means Antigone. A listener who remembers her speech about the laws of Zeus may wonder which of the two has stepped over a line that belongs to him.

s6.quote: Not sleep that lays all else beneath its spell,
s6.note: Sleep is ὁ πάντʼ ἀγρεύων (_ho pant' agreuon_, 'the one who hunts down everything', l. 606), and even he cannot take Zeus. The ode on man ([[s4]]) made man the great hunter, netting birds, beasts and fish. Here the hunting is done to mortals, and the only being beyond the net is a god.

s6.quote: Thou reignest King, omnipotent, sublime.
s6.note: Three English adjectives for one Greek noun, δυνάστας (_dynastas_, 'ruler, potentate', l. 610), who is 'unaged by time' and holds the μαρμαρόεσσαν αἴγλαν (_marmaroessan aiglan_, 'the flashing radiance') of Olympus. The picture is of rule that does not get old. It is sung in front of a king who took power yesterday and whose first decree has already produced a death sentence in his own family.

s6.quote: All bow to thy decree,
s6.note: The Greek word is νόμος (_nomos_, 'law', l. 613): 'for the future and the past this law will hold'. So the play now has three things called law. Creon's proclamation is a _nomos_; Antigone appealed past it to the unwritten _nomima_ of the gods in [[s5]]; and the elders now announce Zeus's law, which is neither a command nor a custom but a regularity, like gravity. It tells you what will happen to the great and nothing about what you ought to do.

s6.quote: All that exceeds the mean by Fate
s6.note: The Greek here (ll. 613-614) is corrupt and much emended, but its drift is: nothing vast, πάμπολύ (_pampoly_), creeps into mortal life ἐκτὸς ἄτας (_ektos atas_, 'outside ruin'). Storr's 'the mean' brings in a doctrine of moderation that the text only implies, and 'Love or Hate' is filler for the rhyme. Still, he catches the elders' philosophy: do not be big. It suits old men who have survived several kings, and it has nothing to say when the moderate course is to leave a brother to the dogs.

s6.quote: Hope flits about never-wearying wings;
s6.note: ἐλπὶς (_elpis_) in Greek is expectation as much as hope, and it is not a comfort. Here it is πολύπλαγκτος (_polyplanktos_, 'far-wandering', l. 615), which Storr turns into a bird. The elders are explaining how ruin gets in: through what people expect to gain. That was Creon's theory of everyone else in [[s3]], where every opponent was after _kerdos_, profit; it will turn out to describe him.

s6.quote: Profit to some, to some light loves she brings,
s6.note: Storr drops the key noun. Hope is a benefit, ὄνασις, to many, but to many it is ἀπάτα κουφονόων ἐρώτων (_apata kouphonoon eroton_, 'the deception of light-minded desires', l. 616). _Apata_ will be heard again within a dozen lines, when Haemon is said to come 'cheated' of his marriage. And 'light-minded' was the ode on man's word for the birds that clever man traps: the trapper is now the bird. With _eroton_ the ode also slips in the subject of the next one ([[s8]]).

s6.quote: Till ’neath his feet the treacherous ashes burn.
s6.note: A man walking over ground he thinks is cold; the Greek says the thing creeps on him 'knowing nothing', εἰδότι δʼ οὐδὲν (l. 617), until he scorches his foot in hot fire. The elders mean it for Antigone, but she knew exactly what she was walking on and said so. The one on stage who does not yet feel the heat is Creon.

s6.quote: Sure ’twas a sage inspired that spake this word;
s6.note: The Chorus now quotes a proverb and says so: a κλεινὸν ἔπος (_kleinon epos_, 'famous saying', l. 620), revealed 'by someone's wisdom'. They do not know whose. This is how the elders think throughout the play: when events become frightening they reach for something everybody already says.

s6.quote: If evil good appear
s6.note: The centre of the ode, and Storr's couplet removes the god from it. The Greek runs: evil seems good to the man whose wits a god is leading towards ruin, φρένας θεὸς ἄγει πρὸς ἄταν (ll. 622-623). The later Latin tag about the gods first maddening those they mean to destroy descends from this thought. The frightening part is that the victim's judgment is the instrument: he does not choose evil knowing it, he sees it as ἐσθλὸν (_esthlon_, 'good, noble'). The elders mean the girl who called a crime holy. Within a hundred lines we will watch a man defend obedience to unjust orders as the highest civic good.

s6.quote: And brief the respite from her flaming sword.
s6.note: The flaming sword comes from Genesis, not Thebes. The Greek is flat and exact: such a man fares 'the briefest time outside ruin', ὀλίγιστον χρόνον ἐκτὸς ἄτας (l. 625). The phrase _ektos atas_ closed the previous stanza too (l. 614), so both halves of the song end on the same two words. Taken as a prediction about Creon it is accurate to the hour: his respite lasts until Tiresias leaves the stage in [[s11]].

s6.quote: Hither comes in angry mood
s6.note: Storr prejudges the entrance. The Greek asks whether Haemon comes ἀχνύμενος (_achnymenos_, 'grieving', l. 627) for Antigone's fate, and the next scene depends on the fact that he arrives perfectly controlled. The metre shifts here from song to marching anapaests, the usual way of announcing a new arrival. The Chorus speaks to Creon, so 'thy brood' is his.

s6.quote: Haemon, latest of thy brood;
s6.note: νέατον γέννημʼ (_neaton gennema_, 'last-born offspring', l. 627). The elders have just sung of the 'last root' of Oedipus's house, and without drawing breath they introduce the last child of Creon's. We learn only at the end ([[s13]]) that another son is already dead. The curse the Chorus thinks it is watching in one family is about to be manufactured, from nothing, in the other.

s6.quote: Or her marriage-bed deceived,
s6.note: ἀπάτης λεχέων (_apates lecheon_, 'the cheating of his marriage-bed', l. 630): the word used a moment ago for the deception worked by light-minded desire (l. 616). The elders have already decided what Haemon's business is. He is a young man in love, deceived of his bride, and whatever he says will be heard as that. Creon makes the same assumption, and Haemon will spend the whole scene refusing to speak in those terms.

s7.quote: Soon shall we know, better than seer can tell.
s7.note: μάντεων ὑπέρτερον (_manteon hyperteron_, 'better than seers', l. 631) is a throwaway idiom, and one of the cruellest ironies in the play. A real seer is coming in [[s11]], and what Creon learns from him he learns one hour too late. For the moment he thinks knowledge is something a king gets by asking a direct question.

s7.quote: Learning may fixed decree anent thy bride,
s7.note: The line is garbled in this printing; read 'my fixed decree'. The Greek is τελείαν ψῆφον (_teleian psephon_, 'the final vote', l. 632). A _psephos_ is the pebble an Athenian dropped in the urn in court or assembly, so Creon dignifies one man's decision with the word for a collective verdict. Haemon will take him at his word and report how the city would actually vote.

s7.quote: Thou mean’st not, son, to rave against thy sire?
s7.note: λυσσαίνων (_lyssainon_, 'raging', l. 633) comes from _lyssa_, the fury of a rabid dog. Creon's first thought about his son is that he may have gone mad. Keep the word in mind: the scene ends with the son telling the father that he is the one who raves (l. 765). The charge of madness travels the whole length of the episode and changes hands.

s7.quote: Know’st not whate’er we do is done in love?
s7.note: Storr softens this. The Greek asks: 'or are we φίλοι (_philoi_, 'dear, your own') to you whatever we do?' (l. 634). It is a demand for unconditional loyalty, made in advance of knowing what has been done. This is Creon's notion of _philia_ throughout: in [[s3]] he chose his friends by their service to the city, and from his son he expects kinship to work as a blank cheque. He means it; he does love his son. The line is unbearable on a second reading.

s7.quote: O father, I am thine, and I will take
s7.note: σός εἰμι (_sos eimi_, 'I am yours', l. 635). Haemon opens with exactly what was asked for, in the fewest possible words. Is it sincere? I think so, and I think it is also strategy: he knows his father, and knows that anything said before these words would not be heard. Nothing in the scene suggests he came intending to quarrel.

s7.quote: Thy wisdom as the helm to steer withal.
s7.note: The Greek is more careful than the English. 'You, having good judgments, set me straight, and those I will follow': γνώμας and χρηστὰς (ll. 635-636). The participle 'having' can mean 'since you have' or 'if you have', and the relative clause promises obedience only to the good ones. Creon hears the first sense. The verb ἀπορθοῖς (_aporthois_, 'you keep straight') belongs to the vocabulary of the upright ship of state from his opening speech in [[s3]], which is why Storr's helm, though his own, is apt.

s7.quote: More precious than thy loving goverance.
s7.note: 'Goverance' is a slip for 'governance', and 'loving' is not in the Greek, which says σοῦ καλῶς ἡγουμένου (_sou kalos hegoumenou_, l. 638): 'you leading well'. Again the grammar leaves a door open: 'since you lead well' or 'so long as you lead well'. Haemon has made two statements of submission and put a condition inside each. The rest of the scene is the condition being called in.

s7.quote: In all deferring to a father’s will.
s7.note: 'To stand behind a father's judgment in everything', ὄπισθεν ἑστάναι (_opisthen hestanai_, l. 640). It is a drill-ground image: the son is posted in the rank behind. Creon cannot describe a family except as a formation, and by the end of this speech the household, the city and the phalanx will have become one thing with one rule.

s7.quote: A brood of sons submissive, keen to avenge
s7.note: Sons are prayed for so that they will be κατηκόους (_katekoous_, 'obedient', literally 'listeners', l. 642), repay the father's ἐχθρὸν (_echthron_, 'enemy') with harm and honour his φίλον (_philon_, 'friend') as he does (ll. 643-644). This is the ordinary Greek ethic of helping friends and harming enemies, but note who decides which is which. A son inherits his father's list. Antigone's list in [[s5]] was fixed by birth; Creon's is fixed by Creon.

s7.quote: But who begets unprofitable sons,
s7.note: ἀνωφέλητα (_anopheleta_, 'useless, bringing no benefit', l. 645). Children are assessed as assets, in the same accounting Creon applies to everyone. The worst consequence he can imagine is γέλων (_gelon_, 'laughter', l. 647) from his enemies, the dread of being mocked that drives Sophoclean heroes. He shares that fear with the girl he has condemned, and neither would thank you for saying so.

s7.quote: And let no woman fool away thy wits.
s7.note: 'Do not throw out your φρένας (_phrenas_, 'wits, good sense') under pleasure, ὑφʼ ἡδονῆς, for a woman's sake' (ll. 648-649). Creon assumes his son's only possible motive is sexual, as the Chorus did when it announced him. Haemon will not say one word about love in the entire scene. Who is thinking about pleasure here is a fair question.

s7.quote: And her embraces very soon wax cold.
s7.note: ψυχρὸν παραγκάλισμα (_psychron parankalisma_, 'a cold thing to hold in your arms', l. 650). Creon means a bad wife. The Messenger in [[s13]] describes Haemon dying with his arms round Antigone's body in the tomb, and the phrase comes true to the letter. Sophocles has given the father the image of his son's death and let him use it as a joke about shrews.

s7.quote: As a false friend? So spue and cast her off,
s7.note: φίλος κακός (_philos kakos_, 'a bad _philos_', l. 652): Antigone is family, Creon's niece and ward, and he has to concede the word even while disowning her. Then πτύσας (_ptysas_, 'spitting', l. 653): spit her out like an enemy. In the tomb, the Messenger reports, Haemon answers his father's pleading by spitting in his face. The gesture Creon prescribes here is the one he will receive.

s7.quote: Bid her go find a husband with the dead.
s7.note: 'Let the girl marry someone in Hades', ἐν Ἅιδου and νυμφεύειν (l. 654). This is where the bride-of-death motif enters the play, as a sneer. Antigone turns it into lament in [[s9]], calling the tomb her bridal chamber, and in [[s13]] it becomes simple fact, when Haemon is said to have got his marriage rites in the house of Hades. Creon never says anything in this scene that the plot does not hold him to.

s7.quote: Of all my subjects the one malcontent,
s7.note: 'Alone out of the whole city', πόλεως and ἐκ πάσης μόνην (l. 656). This is a factual claim, and it is the one Haemon will contradict, first tactfully (the city mourns her, l. 693) and then flatly (the whole people of Thebes denies it, l. 733). Watch the word 'alone', _monos_, through the scene. Creon pins it on Antigone here, and by line 739 it has been pinned on him.

s7.quote: I will not prove a traitor to the State.
s7.note: Storr overstates. The Greek is ψευδῆ (_pseude_, 'false, a liar', l. 657): I will not make myself a liar to the city. Having announced the penalty in public, he cannot now let it lapse, and that, not her guilt, is the reason he gives. It is an honest glimpse of the mechanism: what locks him in is his own proclamation and what it would look like to retreat from it.

s7.quote: She surely dies. Go, let her, if she will,
s7.note: The Greek is two words, ἀλλὰ κτενῶ (_alla kteno_, 'no, I will kill her', l. 658), in the first person. Storr's 'She surely dies' turns an act into an event. Creon himself will retreat to a formula very like Storr's at the end of the scene, when he devises a death in which nobody's hand does the killing.

s7.quote: Appeal to Zeus the God of Kindred, for
s7.note: Δία ξύναιμον (_Dia xynaimon_, 'Zeus of shared blood', ll. 658-659), and the verb is ἐφυμνείτω (_ephymneito_, 'let her chant her hymn to him'), which is contempt. This is the second time Creon has waved away Zeus in his family aspect; in [[s5]] it was Zeus of the household hearth. A man who invokes the gods for the city and mocks them for the family has divided what the Greeks did not divide. The Chorus will use the same adjective of his own quarrel with his son (l. 792).

s7.quote: If thus I nurse rebellion in my house,
s7.note: ἄκοσμα (_akosma_, 'disorderly', l. 660): if I rear my own kin to be without _kosmos_, order. The root returns at l. 677 and l. 730, and it is Creon's master value in this speech, as the city's safety was in [[s3]]. The argument is from the smaller to the larger: indulgence at home will be read as weakness abroad. As political psychology it is not stupid. It is the argument of every ruler who has punished a relative to prove a point.

s7.quote: For whoso rules his household worthily,
s7.note: The man who is χρηστός (_chrestos_, 'sound, good') among his own will be found δίκαιος (_dikaios_, 'just') in the city (ll. 661-662). Set the maxim against the ending: Creon's management of his household costs him his son and his wife within the day. By his own test he stands condemned as a ruler. Some editors rearrange the lines that follow, because the 'such a one' praised at l. 668 fits the obedient man better than the transgressor; Storr translates the transmitted order and the join shows.

s7.quote: But he who overbears the laws, or thinks
s7.note: ὑπερβὰς (_hyperbas_, 'overstepping', l. 663) and νόμους βιάζεται ('does violence to the laws'). The Chorus has just sung that no human _hyperbasia_ can check the power of Zeus (l. 605), and Creon claims the word for offences against his own _nomoi_. The second offence he names is new and aimed at the son in front of him: thinking to give orders to those in power. He has scented advice coming.

s7.quote: Appoints must be obeyed in everything,
s7.note: 'Whomever the πόλις (_polis_) sets up, him one must hear', κλύειν (l. 666). Notice where Creon locates his authority at this stage: in the city's appointment. Seventy lines on he asks with scorn whether the city is to tell him what to order (l. 734). The speech and the stichomythia cannot both be true, and the scene is built to make him say both.

s7.quote: But small and great, just and unjust alike.
s7.note: 'But' looks like a slip in this printing for 'Both'. The Greek is 'in small things and just things and their opposites', καὶ δίκαια καὶ τἀναντία (l. 667); he cannot quite bring himself to say 'unjust' and uses a euphemism. This is the turning point of his case: obedience is owed even to wrong commands. Nothing in his opening speech required this, and nothing after it recovers. It is also the exact position Antigone refused in [[s5|the unwritten laws speech]].

s7.quote: Would shine, as King or subject; such a man
s7.note: καλῶς μὲν ἄρχειν, εὖ δʼ ἂν ἄρχεσθαι (l. 669): to rule well and to be willing to be ruled well. Ruling and being ruled in turn was the Athenian citizen's ideal, and the audience would have nodded. The question the play puts is whether Creon possesses the second half. In this scene he is offered advice by his son, his council and (by report) his people, and treats each offer as mutiny.

s7.quote: A comrade leal and true; but Anarchy—
s7.note: παραστάτην (_parastaten_, 'the man who stands beside you', l. 671) is the hoplite next in the line, whose shield covers your right side. Young Athenians swore in their oath of service not to desert that man. Creon is at his most persuasive here, and it would be a mistake to read the speech as a tyrant's rant. It is the creed of a citizen-soldier whose city was nearly sacked two nights ago.

s7.quote: What evils are not wrought by Anarchy!
s7.note: The Greek is a flat superlative: there is no greater evil than ἀναρχίας (_anarchias_, 'absence of rule', l. 672). Compare the superlatives elsewhere: for Haemon the highest of possessions is good sense (l. 684), and for the Messenger in [[s13]] the worst of evils is bad counsel. The play is partly an argument about what goes at the top of that list, and Creon's answer, disorder, is the only one that makes obedience the supreme virtue.

s7.quote: She ruins States, and overthrows the home,
s7.note: Anarchy makes houses ἀναστάτους (_anastatous_, 'laid waste, emptied', l. 673). Cities, homes, armies: the three institutions fall in one sentence, each introduced by a pointing 'she'. Which house in Thebes is laid waste by nightfall? Creon's, and what empties it is the insistence on rule, not any failure of it.

s7.quote: While discipline preserves the ordered ranks.
s7.note: πειθαρχία (_peitharchia_, 'obedience to command', l. 676) is the opposite pole to _anarchia_, and what it saves is τὰ πολλὰ σώμαθʼ, 'most of the bodies', men's lives. It is a soldier's truth. It is also an awkward noun to hear from a man in a play about a body, whose refusal to release one corpse is about to cost three more.

s7.quote: And yield to title to a woman’s will.
s7.note: Read 'no title'. After forty lines on fathers, cities and armies the speech lands here: γυναικὸς οὐδαμῶς ἡσσητέα (_gynaikos oudamos hessetea_, 'we must on no account be worsted by a woman', l. 678). I think this is the real conclusion and the rest is its justification. In [[s5]] he said no woman would rule while he lived; a principle that needs repeating this often is covering a fear.

s7.quote: Than hear it said, a woman proved his match.
s7.note: Better to fall πρὸς ἀνδρὸς (_pros andros_, 'at a man's hands', l. 679) than be called γυναικῶν ἥσσονες (_gynaikon hessones_, 'weaker than women', l. 680). 'Be called': it is reputation again. He gets the alternative he asks for. He is brought down by men, a son and a blind prophet, and it makes no difference to how far he falls. Haemon will throw the word 'weaker' back at him at l. 747.

s7.quote: To me, unless old age have dulled wits,
s7.note: 'Unless we have been robbed by time', τῷ χρόνῳ κεκλέμμεθα (l. 681), 'you seem to speak sensibly', φρονούντως (_phronountos_, l. 682). The elders endorse Creon with an escape clause already attached. In forty lines they will endorse Haemon as well. Their value as a moral guide in this scene is nil, and their value as a picture of how a council behaves under a strong ruler is considerable.

s7.quote: Reason, the choicest gift bestowed by heaven.
s7.note: Haemon's first word after 'Father' is θεοὶ, 'the gods', and what they plant in men is φρένας (_phrenas_, 'wits, good sense', l. 683), the faculty Creon warned him not to throw away at l. 648. He accepts his father's term and changes its owner: sense is the gods' gift to human beings generally, so no one man holds all of it. He calls it the highest of κτημάτων (_ktematon_, 'possessions', l. 684), meeting Creon's talk of profitable sons in its own currency.

s7.quote: ’Tis not for me to say thou errest, nor
s7.note: This is the tact the scene is famous for. 'That you do not speak ὀρθῶς (_orthos_, 'rightly, straight') I could not say, and may I never know how to' (ll. 685-686). He disclaims both the ability and the wish to criticise, and then criticises for forty lines by reporting what others say. It is how one speaks to a man whose 'eye is terrible': the truth has to arrive as hearsay.

s7.quote: And yet wise thoughts may come to other men
s7.note: γένοιτο μέντἂν χἀτέρῳ καλῶς ἔχον (l. 687): 'yet something good might come to another man too'. The whole speech is in this modest potential clause. Haemon never argues that the burial was right. He argues that a second opinion can exist, and Creon will be unable to grant even that.

s7.quote: And, as thy son, it falls to me to mark
s7.note: προσκοπεῖν (_proskopein_, 'to look out ahead', l. 688) is scouting, and he says he was born to do it for his father. It turns Creon's military idea of the son to a better use than standing in the rear rank. A son who watches on his father's behalf will sometimes see what the father does not want seen. Creon asked for a subordinate who hates his enemies; he is offered an intelligence service.

s7.quote: The commons stand in terror of thy frown,
s7.note: τὸ γὰρ σὸν ὄμμα δεινὸν (_to son omma deinon_, 'your eye is terrible', l. 690) to the ἀνδρὶ δημότῃ, the ordinary man of the people. _Deinos_ is the ode on man's great word, 'formidable, wonderful, dreadful', and here it has only its ugly sense. Antigone told Creon in [[s5]] that the elders would agree with her if fear did not lock their tongues, and he ignored it from her. The defect of one-man rule shown here is practical before it is moral: the ruler stops receiving information.

s7.quote: But I can overhear their muttered plaints,
s7.note: He hears it ὑπὸ σκότου (_hypo skotou_, 'under cover of darkness', l. 692). There is no assembly in this Thebes and nobody speaks in the open; opinion exists only as something overheard. An Athenian audience, used to settling public questions by open debate, is being shown a city that has to whisper.

s7.quote: Know how the people mourn this maiden doomed
s7.note: ὀδύρεται πόλις (_odyretai polis_, 'the city laments', l. 693). Up to now the _polis_ has been Creon's word, the thing he defends against her. Haemon makes it the subject of a verb of mourning for Antigone, in direct reply to 'alone out of the whole city' at l. 656. From this line on the scene's question is who gets to say 'the city'.

s7.quote: For noblest deeds to die the worst of deaths.
s7.note: Three superlatives in two Greek lines: of all women the least deserving, ἀναξιωτάτη, dying most foully, κάκιστʼ, for deeds most glorious, εὐκλεεστάτων (ll. 694-695). The last is from _eukleia_, 'good fame', and it is what Antigone told Creon in [[s5]] she had won by burying her brother. She claimed it defiantly and with no sign that anyone agreed. She never learns that the city gave it to her.

s7.quote: When her own brother slain in battle lay
s7.note: αὐτάδελφον (_autadelphon_, 'her very own brother', l. 696) is the word of the play's first line, where Antigone used it of Ismene. The citizens, as Haemon reports them, describe the deed in her vocabulary and not in Creon's: Polynices is a brother fallen in the slaughter and unburied, with no mention of treason. Dogs that eat flesh raw, ὠμηστῶν κυνῶν (l. 697), keep the physical horror in view, which Creon's abstractions never do.

s7.quote: Should not her name (they cry) be writ in gold?
s7.note: Storr invents the inscription. The Greek asks whether she does not deserve χρυσῆς (_chryses_, 'golden') honour, _time_ (l. 699). This is our only report of what ordinary Thebans think, and it reaches us third-hand through a son with a motive. I believe it anyway, because the elders' chilly 'Thy word is law' in [[s3]] pointed the same way, and because Tiresias in [[s11]] confirms that the city is suffering.

s7.quote: Such the low murmurings that reach my ear.
s7.note: ἐρεμνὴ σῖγʼ ἐπέρχεται φάτις (_eremne sig' eperchetai phatis_, 'a dark rumour comes on in silence', l. 700). Rumour here moves the way ruin moved in the ode just sung, quietly and under cover. Haemon closes the report and turns at once to affection. He knows that this was the dangerous part.

s7.quote: Than thy well-being, for what higher good
s7.note: 'No κτῆμα (_ktema_, 'possession') is more precious to me than your prospering' (ll. 701-702), picking up the 'possessions' of l. 684. A father's good name is his children's ἄγαλμα (_agalma_, 'ornament, glory', l. 704), and theirs is his. It answers Creon's doctrine that sons exist to serve the father's interests by agreeing with it and drawing the right conclusion: your interest is your reputation, and your reputation is going bad in the dark.

s7.quote: Therefore, my father, cling not to one mood,
s7.note: 'Do not wear one single ἦθος (_ethos_, 'cast of mind, character') in yourself', with φόρει (_phorei_, 'carry, wear', l. 705), as one wears a garment. The diagnosis is exact: Creon has one way of being right and puts it on every morning. With μοῦνον, 'one only', the word 'alone' starts to migrate towards him.

s7.quote: That he alone can speak or think aright,
s7.note: φρονεῖν μόνος δοκεῖ (_phronein monos dokei_, 'thinks that he alone has sense', l. 707), or a tongue or a ψυχὴν, a soul, that no one else has. Tongue, soul and thinking: in [[s3]] Creon said you cannot know a man's soul, thought and judgment until he has been tested in office. His son is handing him back his own test.

s7.quote: Such oracles are empty breath when tried.
s7.note: There are no oracles in the Greek. Such men, διαπτυχθέντες (_diaptychthentes_, 'opened up, unfolded', l. 709), like a folded writing-tablet or a box, are seen to be κενοί (_kenoi_, 'empty'). Storr loses the picture of the man as a container with nothing in it. 'Empty' will be traded as an insult later in the scene (ll. 753, 754), and Creon in [[s13]] will call himself a man who no longer exists, no more than nothing.

s7.quote: By others’ wisdom and relax in time.
s7.note: Two infinitives carry the advice: τὸ μανθάνειν (_to manthanein_, 'to learn') and τὸ μὴ τείνειν ἄγαν (_to me teinein agan_, 'not to strain too tight', ll. 710-711). 'Learn' is the play's last idea; its closing lines say that the proud are taught good sense in old age, by blows. 'Strain' sets up the two images that follow, since the tree that 'strains against' the current and the sailor who 'strains' his sheet use the same verb.

s7.quote: See how the trees beside a stream in flood
s7.note: The trees that ὑπείκει (_hypeikei_, 'give way', l. 713) beside the winter torrent save their twigs. A few minutes ago the elders sang of a sea-storm no one could resist and a family cut down to the root; Haemon offers flood and tree again, but as a situation in which there is still a choice. The image should sound familiar to Creon. In [[s5]] he told Antigone that the stiffest wills fall hardest and the hardest iron snaps, and he does not recognise his own argument when it comes back.

s7.quote: But by resisting perish root and branch.
s7.note: ἀντιτείνοντʼ (_antiteinont'_, 'straining against') and αὐτόπρεμνʼ (_autopremn'_, 'trunk and all', l. 714). The ode spoke of the 'last root' of Oedipus's house (l. 600); now the phrase is held out to Creon as a warning about his own. It is prophecy in a strict sense. He loses the whole tree, son and wife and the son before, and survives as the stump.

s7.quote: The mariner who keeps his mainsheet taut,
s7.note: πόδα (_poda_, literally 'foot', l. 715) is the sheet, the rope at the sail's lower corner, kept ἐγκρατῆ, 'under tight control'. The choice of a ship is pointed. Creon introduced himself in [[s3]] as the helmsman of the city, the vessel that keeps everyone safe if it sails upright. His son accepts the metaphor and tells him he does not know how to sail.

s7.quote: To sail with thwarts reversed, keel uppermost.
s7.note: The Greek has a grim joke that Storr keeps: he capsizes and 'voyages for the rest of the trip', τὸ λοιπὸν and ναυτίλλεται, with his rowing-benches upside down, ὑπτίοις and σέλμασιν (ll. 716-717). The tree was about the ruler; the ship has a crew. If the man at the sheet will not ease it, everyone aboard goes into the water with him.

s7.quote: Relent then and repent thee of thy wrath;
s7.note: εἶκε (_eike_, 'yield', l. 718) is the third appearance of the verb in six lines, and the first direct imperative Haemon has allowed himself. He asks for a μετάστασιν (_metastasin_, 'change, shift') in his father's θυμῷ (_thymoi_, 'temper'). Creon does yield, in [[s11]], to the Chorus, in almost these terms. Why can he do for the elders, an hour later, what he cannot do for his son now? Partly fear of Tiresias, and partly, I think, that the elders are old.

s7.quote: With absolute wisdom; but, if that’s denied,
s7.note: The close paraphrases Hesiod, who in the _Works and Days_ ranks the man who thinks everything out for himself first and the man who listens to good advice second, with the man who does neither called useless. Haemon discreetly leaves out the third. He ends on μανθάνειν (_manthanein_, 'to learn', l. 723) again, and prefaces it with an apology for being young (l. 719), having guessed which objection is coming.

s7.quote: Heed thou thy sire too; both have spoken well.
s7.note: εὖ γὰρ εἴρηται διπλῇ (_eu gar eiretai diplei_, 'it has been well said on both sides', l. 725). The two speeches are not compatible: one says obey in everything, the other says the order is wrong and the city knows it. The elders' evenhandedness is a refusal to judge, and it removes the one restraint that might have worked on Creon, a clear word from his council.

s7.quote: Lessoned in prudence by a beardless boy?
s7.note: διδαξόμεσθα and φρονεῖν (_didaxomestha_, _phronein_, 'shall we be taught to have sense', ll. 726-727) by a man of his age? Creon answers none of the arguments. He answers the speaker's birth certificate. The last lines of the play will say that good sense is taught in old age by great blows, so the question he asks in scorn gets a literal yes.

s7.quote: Weigh me upon my merit, not my years.
s7.note: Look at τἄργα (_targa_, 'the deeds, the facts', l. 729), not at my age. From here the scene is in stichomythia, one line each for thirty lines, which in Greek tragedy is the form for a quarrel that has stopped being a discussion. Each speaker takes a word from the other's line and turns it, and you can follow the whole exchange by the stolen words.

s7.quote: Strange merit this to sanction lawlessness!
s7.note: Creon takes 'deed' and twists it: is it a deed to σέβειν (_sebein_, 'revere') those who are disorderly, τοὺς ἀκοσμοῦντας (l. 730)? _Sebein_ is religious vocabulary, the word for what one owes the gods, and it now enters the quarrel and will not leave: ll. 731, 744, 745, 777, 780. The question of the play, what deserves reverence, is being fought out in a single verb.

s7.quote: For evil-doers I would urge no plea.
s7.note: 'I would not ask you to show piety towards the wicked', εὐσεβεῖν and κακούς (l. 731). Haemon gives up nothing here. He grants the principle and denies that it applies to her. He is still arguing; the anger has not started.

s7.quote: Is not this maid an arrant law-breaker?
s7.note: Storr drops the metaphor. Creon asks whether she has not been seized by such a νόσῳ (_nosoi_, 'disease', l. 732). Wrongdoing as sickness is his habit of speech, and it rebounds: Tiresias will tell him in [[s11]] that the city is sick and that the source is his own mind.

s7.quote: The Theban commons with one voice say, No.
s7.note: ὁμόπτολις λεώς (_homoptolis leos_, 'the people who share this city', l. 733). _Homoptolis_ is a rare word, 'of the same polis', and it is chosen to make the point that the city is a thing held in common. Haemon has dropped the hearsay and the tact. This is a flat statement of fact against his father's flat statement at l. 656.

s7.quote: What, shall the mob dictate my policy?
s7.note: The Greek word is πόλις (_polis_, l. 734), and Storr's 'mob' badly obscures what happens. Creon does not sneer at a rabble. He asks whether the city is to tell him what orders to give. The man whose whole case was the city's safety and the city's appointment (l. 666) now sets himself against the city by name. This is the line where the polis and the one man come apart, and he is the one who separates them.

s7.quote: ’Tis thou, methinks, who speakest like a boy.
s7.note: ἄγαν νέος (_agan neos_, 'altogether too young', l. 735). Haemon returns the taunt of l. 727. It is fair: the idea that the ruler owes no account to anyone is an adolescent's idea of power, and Creon is new to the job. It is also the moment the son stops managing his father and starts scoring off him.

s7.quote: Am I to rule for others, or myself?
s7.note: The Greek dative is ambiguous between 'by another's judgment' and 'for another's benefit' (l. 736), and Creon means both: this land is to be ruled, ἄρχειν χθονός, by him and for him. Notice that 'city' has become 'land'. He is talking about territory he holds.

s7.quote: A State for one man is no State at all.
s7.note: 'That is no πόλις (_polis_) which belongs to one man', ἀνδρός and ἑνός (l. 737). An Athenian audience, proud of governing itself, would have gone with this line at once. Haemon has shifted the ground from what his father may forbid to whose city it is. It is a definition, and by it Creon's Thebes has ceased to be a city while he was speaking.

s7.quote: The State is his who rules it, so ’tis held.
s7.note: 'Is the city not considered to belong to the one in power?', τοῦ κρατοῦντος and νομίζεται (l. 738). The verb is from _nomos_: it is 'customarily held'. So here, at the bottom of the argument, is Creon's _nomos_: the city is property. In [[s3]] it was a ship carrying everyone, and its safety was the measure of a man. The audience has watched a decent political creed turn into ownership in the course of one day.

s7.quote: As monarch of a desert thou wouldst shine.
s7.note: 'You would rule well, alone, over an empty land', ἐρήμης and μόνος (l. 739). The deferential son is gone and this is sarcasm. _Monos_, 'alone', which Creon fixed on Antigone at l. 656, has come home to him. It is also prophecy: by the end he rules a palace with nobody left in it, and within forty lines he will send Antigone to a place he calls by the same word, 'desolate' (l. 773).

s7.quote: This boy, methinks, maintains the woman’s cause.
s7.note: Beaten on the city, Creon changes ground to gender, and changes addressee: 'this fellow' is said to the Chorus, over his son's head. συμμαχεῖ (_symmachei_, 'fights as ally of', l. 740) is military. At l. 674 anarchy was what broke the allied spear, and Creon now files his son under the enemy's alliance.

s7.quote: If thou be’st woman, yes. My thought’s for thee.
s7.note: εἴπερ γυνὴ σύ (_eiper gyne sy_, 'if you are a woman', l. 741). A hit at the sorest point, since being bested by a woman is the thing Creon cannot bear, and then at once the truth of the scene: σοῦ and προκήδομαι, 'it is you I am anxious for'. I believe him. The speech was not a lover's plea in disguise, and reading it that way is Creon's mistake and the Chorus's.

s7.quote: O reprobate, would’st wrangle with thy sire?
s7.note: διὰ δίκης ἰὼν (_dia dikes ion_, 'going to law with', l. 742) your father. Creon takes disagreement for litigation, a son suing his parent, which in Greek eyes is monstrous. The word _dike_, justice, has entered, and Haemon uses it against him in the next line.

s7.quote: Because I see thee wrongfully perverse.
s7.note: οὐ γὰρ δίκαιά (_ou gar dikaia_, 'not just', l. 743): I see you going wrong against justice. For the first time Haemon says in his own voice what he began by saying he could never say (l. 685). The verb for erring, here and in Creon's reply, gives the noun Creon will use of his own mistakes in his lament in [[s13]].

s7.quote: And am I wrong, if I maintain my rights?
s7.note: τὰς ἐμὰς ἀρχὰς σέβων (_tas emas archas sebon_, 'revering my own office', l. 744). The reverence verb again, with Creon's own authority as its object. Storr's 'rights' is too modern and too mild. Creon is describing a piety, and the god it is paid to is his position.

s7.quote: Talk not of rights; thou spurn’st the due of Heaven
s7.note: 'You do not revere, οὐ γὰρ σέβεις, when you trample the honours of the gods', τιμάς and πατῶν (l. 745). This is the first time Haemon makes the religious charge, forty lines after a speech that kept the gods out of it except as givers of sense. He has reached Antigone's position by a different road. The verb 'trample' is physical and is meant to be.

s7.quote: O heart corrupt, a woman’s minion thou!
s7.note: μιαρὸν ἦθος (_miaron ethos_, 'polluted character', l. 746). _Miaros_ belongs with _miasma_, religious defilement, and Creon throws it at his son as abuse. Thirty lines later he is taking careful steps to keep _miasma_ off the city (l. 776). The actual pollution, as Tiresias will report, comes from the corpse he left out, and it is on every altar in Thebes.

s7.quote: Slave to dishonor thou wilt never find me.
s7.note: ἥσσω (_hesso_, 'weaker than, beaten by', l. 747): you will not catch me giving in to what is shameful, τῶν αἰσχρῶν. He picks up his father's word from l. 680, 'weaker than women', and corrects its object. Being beaten by a woman is not a disgrace; giving in to a base act is.

s7.quote: And thee and me, and for the gods below.
s7.note: Creon says the whole speech was for her; Haemon adds three more clients, 'you, and me, and the gods below', θεῶν τῶν νερτέρων (l. 749). The phrase is the Chorus's from the ode (l. 601), where the nether gods' dust cut down the last root. It is an exact list of who is injured by what Creon is doing, in the order in which he will find it out last.

s7.quote: Living the maid shall never be thy bride.
s7.note: 'You shall never marry her while she still lives', ἔτι ζῶσαν (l. 750). Creon means it as a simple veto and builds the loophole himself. Haemon marries her dead: the Messenger in [[s13]] says he lies corpse embracing corpse, having won his marriage rites in Hades' house.

s7.quote: So she shall die, but one will die with her.
s7.note: The Greek is more open than Storr: θανοῦσʼ ὀλεῖ τινα (_thanous' olei tina_, 'in dying she will destroy someone', l. 751). Haemon means himself. Creon assumes he is being threatened, since by now he hears every sentence as an attack on his authority. He is not wholly wrong: in the tomb Haemon draws his sword on his father first, misses, and only then turns it on himself. The indefinite 'someone' covers both, and Sophocles surely chose it for that.

s7.quote: What threat is this, vain counsels to reprove?
s7.note: κενὰς γνώμας (_kenas gnomas_, 'empty judgments', l. 753). 'Empty' is Haemon's word from l. 709 for the man who thinks he alone has sense, now applied without disguise. At l. 635 he promised to follow his father's judgments, _gnomas_, provided they were good. This is the proviso being exercised.

s7.quote: Vain fool to instruct thy betters; thou shall rue it.
s7.note: Creon catches both words and throws them back: 'you will teach sense in tears, being yourself empty of sense', φρενώσεις and κενός (l. 754). The quarrel has shrunk to two men each telling the other he has no _phrenes_. The ode's proverb was that a god leads the wits of the doomed man towards ruin, and the audience is being invited to decide whose wits those are.

s7.quote: Wert not my father, I had said thou err’st.
s7.note: 'I would have said you are not in your right mind', οὐκ εὖ φρονεῖν (_ouk eu phronein_, l. 755). He says it by saying he will not. Set this beside l. 685, where he prayed never to know how to say such a thing, and you have the measure of how far the scene has travelled in seventy lines.

s7.quote: Play not the spaniel, thou a woman’s slave.
s7.note: δούλευμα (_douleuma_, 'slave-thing', l. 756) is a neuter abstract, a chattel and not a person, and κώτιλλέ (_kotille_) means to wheedle or chatter. Creon has now called his son an ally of a woman, lower than a woman, and a woman's property. Three times is a pattern: gender is where he goes whenever an argument has cornered him.

s7.quote: When thou dost speak, must no man make reply?
s7.note: 'Do you want to speak and, having spoken, hear nothing?', λέγειν and κλύειν (l. 757). It is the best short description of Creon in the play. 'Hearing' was what he required of the citizen (l. 666) and of sons, who should be 'listeners' (l. 642). Haemon's point is that the verb ought to work in both directions.

s7.quote: Off with the hateful thing that she may die
s7.note: Creon swears by Olympus (l. 758), the seat of the Zeus the Chorus has just hymned, and calls for Antigone as τὸ μῖσος (_to misos_, 'the hatred, the hateful thing', l. 760), another neuter. The order is given to attendants and is not carried out before Haemon leaves. Up to this line the scene has been an argument; this is a decision to hurt.

s7.quote: At once, beside her bridegroom, in his sight.
s7.note: κατʼ ὄμματʼ (_kat' ommat'_, 'before his eyes') and νυμφίῳ (_nymphioi_, 'bridegroom', ll. 760-761), the word spat out. The father proposes to kill the bride in front of the groom as a punishment for arguing. What happens is the mirror of it: the bridegroom dies beside the bride, before the father's eyes. Every cruelty Creon devises in this scene is returned to him with the roles changed.

s7.quote: Or by my side; never shalt thou again
s7.note: 'You will never look on my face with your eyes', προσόψει (l. 764). It sounds like a vow of exile or of suicide, and Haemon may not know which. It is also untrue, and the play needs it to be: Creon sees him once more, alive, in the tomb, where the son looks at him 'with wild eyes' and says nothing. These are the last words we hear Haemon speak.

s7.quote: With friends who like a madman for their mate.
s7.note: μαίνῃ (_mainei_, 'you rave, you are mad', l. 765): rave on, among such of your φίλων (_philon_) as can bear it. The scene opened with the father asking whether the son came raging (l. 633) and whether the two were still _philoi_ (l. 634). It closes with the son answering both. Haemon goes out by the side passage towards the country, not into the palace; the audience is given no idea where, and neither is Creon.

s7.quote: Fell is the wrath of youth beneath a smart.
s7.note: He has gone ἐξ ὀργῆς ταχύς (_ex orges tachys_, 'swift from anger', l. 766), and a mind so young, when hurt, is βαρύς (_barys_, 'heavy, dangerous', l. 767). _Orge_, temper, is the ode on man's word for the civic disposition and Creon's ruling fault. The elders see the danger clearly and say it. They said nothing useful while he was on stage, and the same pattern returns in [[s13]] with Eurydice, whose silent exit they also remark on too late.

s7.quote: Let him go vent his fury like a fiend:
s7.note: No fiend in the Greek: 'let him do it, let him go and think thoughts greater than befit a man', φρονείτω μεῖζον ἢ κατʼ ἄνδρʼ (l. 768). Thinking beyond mortal measure is the standard Greek description of the offence the gods punish. Creon diagnoses it in a son who asked him to listen to other people, and he is, at this moment, the play's chief case of it.

s7.quote: These sisters twain he shall not save from death.
s7.note: The Greek uses the dual number, τὼ and κόρα (_to kora_, 'the two girls', l. 769). Ismene, who did nothing, is still under sentence from [[s5]]. Creon has not thought about her since; she is simply included, as part of a pair.

s7.quote: I stand corrected; only her who touched
s7.note: One mild question from the Chorus and Ismene is reprieved: 'not the one who did not touch it', θιγοῦσαν, 'you are right', εὖ γὰρ οὖν λέγεις (l. 771). Two things follow. Her sentence was temper and nothing else. And Creon can be turned by a single line when it comes from old men and costs him nothing, which makes his deafness to Haemon a matter of who was speaking. It is the elders' one successful intervention before [[s11]], and they do not try a second.

s7.quote: She shall be taken to some desert place
s7.note: ἔρημος (_eremos_, 'deserted', l. 773), Haemon's word from l. 739 for the land Creon is fit to rule. The edict announced death by public stoning ([[s1]]). Why the change? Stoning needs the hands of the citizens, and Creon has just been told that the citizens are on her side. I think the new sentence is a silent admission that Haemon's report was true.

s7.quote: By man untrod, and in a rock-hewn cave,
s7.note: κρύψω and ζῶσαν (_krypso_, _zosan_, 'I will hide her, living', l. 774). The verb is the ordinary one for covering the dead with earth. So the decree that kept a dead man above ground ends by putting a living woman below it. Tiresias states the inversion to Creon's face in [[s11]], as the offence against both sets of gods.

s7.quote: With food no more than to avoid the taint
s7.note: The ration is a legal fiction: if she starves with food beside her, the city has not shed kindred blood. The Greek has two technical terms, ἄγος (_agos_, here 'what discharges the guilt', l. 775) and μίασμα (_miasma_, 'pollution', l. 776), which the whole city is to escape. Creon, who scoffed at the gods' interest in a corpse, turns out to be scrupulous about ritual when it protects him. The care is real and wholly misdirected: the pollution is already in the city, spreading from the unburied body.

s7.quote: The King of Death, the one god she reveres,
s7.note: 'Hades, whom alone of gods she reveres', μόνον σέβει θεῶν (l. 777). A taunt, and a false one: she appealed to Zeus and to Justice in [[s5]]. But it fixes how Creon sees the conflict, as his gods of the city against her god of the dead. The play will say that this division of the gods into parties is the mistake.

s7.quote: ’Tis labor lost, to reverence the dead.
s7.note: πόνος περισσός (_ponos perissos_, 'wasted, excessive labour', l. 780). _Perissos_ was Ismene's word in [[s1]] for the senselessness of doing too much. The scene's last word in Greek is σέβειν (_sebein_, 'to revere'), the verb the two men have fought over since l. 730. Creon expects Antigone to learn this lesson in the cave. He learns its opposite at the cave mouth.

s8.note: Ἔρως ἀνίκατε μάχαν (_Eros anikate machan_, 'Eros, unconquered in battle', l. 781). The scene just ended was about winning: Creon would not be 'worsted' by a woman, and no one has given way. The Chorus now names the one combatant nobody beats. Ask what they are doing by singing this now. A girl has just been sentenced to be walled up alive, a son has left in despair, and the elders sing a hymn to desire. It lets them explain the quarrel without judging it.

s8.quote: all yield at a glance of thine eye,
s8.note: Storr's own line. The Greek says something odder: Eros 'who falls upon possessions', ἐν κτήμασι πίπτεις (l. 781), like a raider. _Ktemata_ was Haemon's word twice in [[s7]], for good sense as the best of possessions and for his father's welfare as his own. I hear the Chorus picking it up: love descends on what men own and value, and makes havoc of it.

s8.quote: Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie,
s8.note: The one soft picture in a hard ode: Eros who ἐννυχεύεις (_ennycheueis_, 'keep the night watch', l. 782) on the μαλακαῖς παρειαῖς (_malakais pareiais_, 'soft cheeks') of a girl. Even here the verb is a sentry's. The Greek names Eros, and later Aphrodite; Storr makes both 'Love'. The girl we are about to see has no such nights ahead of her.

s8.quote: Over the upland holds. Shall mortals not yield to thee?
s8.note: Storr drops half the range. Eros roams ὑπερπόντιος (_hyperpontios_, 'over the sea', l. 785) and among the dwellings of the wild country, and no immortal can escape him, nor any of mankind, the creatures of a day. Sea and wilderness are exactly the realms man was praised for mastering in the ode on man ([[s4]]). This song is its correction: there is a power abroad in both that has not been tamed, and the gods are subject to it as well.

s8.quote: Mad are thy subjects all, and even the wisest heart
s8.note: ὁ δʼ ἔχων μέμηνεν (_ho d' echon memenen_, 'he who has you is mad', l. 790). Haemon's parting word to his father was 'rave' (l. 765); the elders quietly hand the madness back to Haemon. And 'wisest' is wrong: the Greek says Eros wrenches aside the minds of the δικαίων (_dikaion_, 'the just') and makes them ἀδίκους (_adikous_, 'unjust', l. 791). That is a verdict. In their view a good son has been made to do wrong.

s8.quote: Straight to folly will fall, at a touch of thy poisoned dart.
s8.note: The dart belongs to a later Cupid. The Greek says the just are dragged aside ἐπὶ λώβᾳ (_epi lobai_, 'to their ruin, to their disgrace', l. 791), and the verb παρασπᾷς (_paraspais_) is to jerk a horse off its line. Here I part company with the Chorus. Haemon made a political argument and never mentioned love, and the city, by his account, agrees with him. Calling it Eros turns a case that needed answering into a fever that only needs explaining.

s8.quote: Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin,
s8.note: νεῖκος ἀνδρῶν ξύναιμον (_neikos andron xynaimon_, 'this quarrel of men of one blood', l. 792). _Xynaimon_ is the epithet Creon sneered at when he told Antigone to go and chant to Zeus of kindred blood (ll. 658-659). And _neikos_, 'strife', is the word inside the name Polynices, a pun the entry song made in [[s2]]. The war of brothers is over and the same strife has moved one generation and one household along. The elders' diagnosis lets them avoid asking which of the two was right, a question they dodged a moment ago by saying both had spoken well.

s8.quote: By the eyes of a winsome wife,
s8.note: 'Victory goes to the desire that shines plain from the eyes of the bride', νικᾷ and ἵμερος (_nikai_, _himeros_, l. 795). 'Wins' answers 'unconquered' in the first line. The bride is νύμφας (_nymphas_, l. 796), and she is εὐλέκτρου (_eulektrou_), 'of the happy marriage-bed'. Nothing in the play has shown us Antigone as an object of desire, and she has not spoken Haemon's name. The elders supply a love story from the outside, and then she walks in.

s8.quote: For as her consort still, enthroned with Justice above,
s8.note: A notorious crux; the text is doubted. As it stands, desire sits πάρεδρος (_paredros_, 'seated beside', as an assessor sits beside a magistrate) in rule with the great θεσμῶν (_thesmon_, 'ordinances', ll. 796-800). Storr's 'Justice' stands for those ordinances. If the reading is right it is an astonishing claim: desire holds office alongside the fundamental laws. The play has had Creon's _nomos_ and Antigone's unwritten _nomima_, and the Chorus now seats a third power on the same bench.

s8.quote: Thou bendest man to thy will, O all invincible Love.
s8.note: The Greek names her: ἄμαχος γὰρ ἐμπαίζει θεὸς Ἀφροδίτα (_amachos gar empaizei theos Aphrodita_, 'for the goddess Aphrodite, not to be fought, has her sport', l. 800). Storr loses the name and, worse, the verb. _Empaizei_ is to play, to mock. The ode ends by saying that the catastrophe gathering over two houses is, from where the goddess sits, a game.

s8.quote: Lo I myself am borne aside,
s8.note: The metre changes to anapaests as Antigone is brought out under guard. The elders have sung that Eros drags the just off their course, and now 'I myself am carried outside the ordinances', θεσμῶν and ἔξω φέρομαι (ll. 801-802), by pity. Which ordinances? I take them to be the loyalty they owe the king. It is their most honest line so far, and it changes nothing they do.

s8.quote: (O sight an eye in tears to drown)
s8.note: They can no longer hold back the πηγὰς (_pegas_, 'springs', l. 803) of their tears. Mark who is weeping: the men who told Creon his speech was sensible and who have just set the girl's rescue down to a young man's lust. The tears are real. They are also the cheapest thing the elders have to give, and they give nothing else until Tiresias has frightened them.

s8.quote: Death’s bower with the dead to share.
s8.note: τὸν παγκοίτην and θάλαμον (_ton pankoiten thalamon_, 'the chamber where all are laid to sleep', l. 804). A _thalamos_ is a bedroom, above all the bridal chamber, and Storr's 'bower' keeps that. So the hymn to Eros ends by handing its bride to death, and the image Creon coined as a sneer ('let her marry someone in Hades') is now the Chorus's pity. Antigone takes it over herself in [[s9]], where her whole lament is the lament of a bride.
